item.content:encoded:
From Axis of Ordinary — Links for 2026-11-20
METR measures rapid gains on its task suites
METR estimates that the human task duration at which models succeed half the time doubled about every 3.6 months across two benchmark suites. Models often matched or beat skilled people on coding and optimization with clear feedback, but showed weaker judgment when feedback was slow or incomplete. Direct human baselines accounted for only 9% of task-duration estimates. The evaluation measures skills relevant to AI research and development and leaves open how much models will accelerate real research.

item.content:encoded: From Axis of Ordinary — Links for 2026-11-20: Independent checkers accept Claude-assisted Riemann proof — Levent Alpöge released a Lean proof of the classical Riemann hypothesis and its generalization to Dirichlet L-functions, developed with Claude. Andrew Sutherland reports that the five headline theorems use only Lean's three standard axioms and that the independent nanoda checker accepted the full proof. Later checks in the Lean community also succeeded. In his commentary, Scott Aaronson argues that mathematicians still have to distill the ideas into an argument people can read and reuse.

item.content:encoded: From Axis of Ordinary — Links for 2026-11-20, A preprint claims blowup in unforced Navier–Stokes: Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster’s AI-assisted preprint claims that a smooth solution to the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations can develop a singularity in finite time without external forcing. The public Lean package omits the numerical certificate and the computation used to validate it. The repository also says the patched package had yet to be rebuilt. item.title: Statistics: The False Discovery Rate — Daily Learning
item.description: Test 100 betting angles and 20 come back "significant" at a 5% false discovery rate, and expect about 1 of those 20 winners to be a mirage, since the rate is the expected share of claimed discoveries that are false positives. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure is the standard way to hold that share in check, which is why genomics, A/B testing, and quant research lean on it when thousands of tests…
item.content:encoded: Test 100 betting angles and 20 come back "significant" at a 5% false discovery rate, and expect about 1 of those 20 winners to be a mirage, since the rate is the expected share of claimed discoveries that are false positives. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure is the standard way to hold that share in check, which is why genomics, A/B testing, and quant research lean on it when thousands of tests run at once.

item.title: Quantum microscope reads atoms' spins in color in one shot
item.description: ICFO researchers imaged individual strontium-87 atoms and distinguished all ten of their spin states in a single experimental run. A laser tuned to strontium's red narrow-line transition excites only one spin state at a time, so each state fluoresces in its own color while the other nine stay dark.

item.title: Daily movement beats age as a longevity predictor
item.description: A study of 3,600 adults found that daily movement, measured by a wrist tracker, predicted longevity better than age, diabetes or heart disease. The catch is that consumer wearables report proprietary activity scores, so it is unclear whether those scores carry the same predictive value as the raw data the researchers used.

item.title: Homo erectus lived in rainforests as recently as 184,000 years ago
item.description: Strontium in the tooth enamel suggests some individuals ranged up to 250 kilometers through forested karst while their teeth were forming. A ninth tooth fits neither Homo erectus, Homo sapiens nor Neanderthals, hinting it may be Denisovan or a hybrid.

item.title: Quantum physics can verify a person's location
item.description: NIST researchers demonstrated that quantum physics can verify a person's location, reporting the first complete demonstration of the protocol on November 18 in Nature. Two verifying stations 195 meters apart on the NIST campus in Boulder used entangled photons and response timing to confirm where the prover stood.

item.title: Eagles preyed on human-sized baboons
item.description: Skulls and bones of adult male baboons found in Chad's Ennedi plateau bore talon punctures and rake marks, with one animal estimated at over 26 kg. It overturns the assumption that hominin-sized ancestors had escaped eagle predation for the past 2.5 million years.
